data.engine#engine: The pure-Go (CGO_ENABLED=0) TeX engine. A faithful re-implementation of TeX that loads and runs the genuine LaTeX classes — \documentclass{article}, {report} and {book} execute the real, embedded .cls files (LPPL, verbatim) — not an emulation — in native builds and in the browser via js/wasm, with no TeXLive and no server.
data.fidelity-gates#Fidelity gates:
a byte-exact conformance ratchet (TestConformance), TeX snippets checked byte-for-byte against real-TeX output; and
a whole-document prose fidelity check against a real LaTeX engine (tectonic). On a corpus of 154 real arXiv papers with a reference PDF each, a vocabulary-bounded word census puts the median at 101% of the reference engine’s prose words (measured 2026-10-04); 10 of the 154 fall below 95% and 3 below 90%. Pagination lands on the reference exactly for 32 of them, with a total page deviation of 304 over the corpus (v0.261.0, font-controlled).
In the default configuration — a different measurement, not an update of the one above, and the two must not be mixed — v0.263.0 lands exactly on 36 of the 154 with Σ|deviation| 294 and a signed bias of +72 pages. The bias is where the work is: it is a one-column phenomenon (#622), and v0.263.0 took 7 pages off it by keeping page_total and page_depth apart in the page builder. A page whose material reached exactly \textheight had been refused over the descender of its own last line, and lost a line (tex.web 19519-19529, 19594-19599).
The bias now has attributable causes rather than a shape. They were found by building documents that carry one ingredient and counting pages against the reference: 300 one-line paragraphs, 80 prose paragraphs and 40 \sections all come out equal, and it is those equalities that make the two that differ attributable. 40 display equations cost a page too many — fixed in v0.267.0 — and 40 itemize blocks still do, with every height agreeing, which puts that one in the page breaking rather than in the spacing (#685). None of these probes needs two paginations to be aligned, which is why they could answer where the alignment-based instruments could not: across the corpus only 6 of 154 documents have a first divergence that is attributable at all, and none agrees with the reference on every comparable page.
A median above 100% is expected rather than flattering: the engine emits each formula’s source as an invisible text layer so that maths can be found, copied and read aloud, and the census counts it. The figure to watch is the tail — the papers below 95% — not the median.
That text layer is also why a PDF text extractor cannot be used to check mathematics against another engine: on a formula it returns our source, not glyph positions, so it compares two different things. Use the vector output, or the engine’s own box metrics, when the question is how a formula is set. v0.263.1 is not measured in these terms yet. It carries the spacing and breaking work described above, and the one piece of it measured on its own — \\ no longer ejecting a page in vertical mode — moved Σ|deviation| from 294 to 283, the bias from +72 to +59, and the exact papers from 36 to 39. That figure belongs to that change against its own control, not to the release: a sum assembled from separate deltas drifts, so the release’s own number is left blank until the release itself is swept.
v0.265.0 was swept whole, which is the only way one of these numbers earns its place: 154 documents in the default configuration, Σ|deviation| 276, signed bias +50, 38 exact. It is not comparable to the 294/+72/36 above, which was measured at v0.263.0 on the same corpus but before the footnote work; the figures that are comparable are its own control — the commit immediately before the last of the four, which already carried the other three — at 277/+49/38. That control is not v0.264.0, and saying so matters: v0.264.0 predates all four changes, so a reader who took it for the baseline would credit this release with work three earlier merges had already done.
v0.267.0 moves the figure the bias is about. A display now chooses between the long and the short pair of skips as tex.web:22578-22585 does, and on the same sweep the signed bias falls +50 → +35 with the median absolute deviation reaching 0. Σ|deviation| moves only 276 → 275, and that is the number to read beside it: every document the change moved got shorter, by the right amount, which rights the eight we set too long and worsens six we already set too short — two of them from exact. The surplus glue had been cancelling a second, opposite error, which is now measurable on its own (engine#683). A figure of merit that improves while its own components get worse is worth printing both ways.
And then the bias turned out to be one rule, which was ours and not TeX’s. build_page never compares page_total to page_goal. It runs until the contribution list is empty (tex.web:19425-19432) and fires the page only when a breakpoint costs awful_bad, which is reached at :19598 when page_total - page_goal > page_shrink. A page is full when its excess beats the glue it can shrink away, not when it is taller than \vsize. This engine’s page breaker carried a second rule of its own — return as soon as page_total crossed \vsize, at whatever node happened to cross it — so every page whose glue could have been tightened stopped one item short.
The sign had been visible for weeks without being read: page_shrink was accumulated at every glue node and a whole branch of the badness function existed for “too tall but recoverable”, and neither was ever reached. A quantity ported from the reference, maintained at every step and never consulted, is the witness of an extra rule, not of a useless quantity.
Removing it broke two tests, which was the right signal rather than a reason to stop: with build_page’s rule alone, a page that overflows with no breakpoint after it never fires. tex.web:20486-20500 is how TeX gets there — \end appends \hbox to \hsize{}, \vfill and \penalty-'10000000000 and runs build_page once more, so the last page is decided at a real breakpoint like every other. With that rule in, both tests pass again with their original expectations: it reproduces the old answer everywhere the old answer was right and differs only where there is shrink to spend.
On the same sweep: signed bias +35 → −1, exact papers 39 → 46, Σ|deviation| 275 → 273 (engine#693). Σ moving by two while the bias moves by thirty-six means documents moved in both directions, and they did: of the 24 that moved, sixteen improved and seven got worse, two of them from exact. Every one of those seven is a document we already set shorter than the reference, which is now the open figure (engine#695).
What that bias had been paying for. Three changes transcribed faithfully from latex.ltx had been measured as regressions against it — \addpenalty on lists, \addvspace, and the sectioning penalties — and all three are negative penalties, so all three shortened documents and all three scored against a baseline that was 35 pages too long. Re-measured on the corrected builder, \addvspace gives the same −8 it always gave: it read as a gain of 8 at +35 and reads as a loss of 8 at −1. It never moved anything toward the reference. While a baseline carries a bias, every change that shares its direction is paid for it.
v0.271.0: Σ|deviation| 273 → 272, exact 46 → 47, signed bias −1 → −12. Twelve merges, and the bias is where they show: \vspace* restoring \prevdepth (#706), \splitmaxdepth and \boxmaxdepth at \maxdimen (#702), a forced break that does not get to choose on an already-overfull page (#701).
And most of that release is invisible to these three numbers. They count pages. A kern, or a heading set at 14.4pt instead of 14, moves glyphs inside a line and costs a page only when it tips one. Measured with hashdiff, which hashes the rendered page instead of counting it:
change renders that differ movement in Σ GPOS kerning accumulates (#715) 2 of 154 0 the size ladder is exact (#718) 124 of 154 0 an [11pt] class at 10.95 (#719) 22 of 154 −1, one document to exact running heads get their marks (#729) 6 of 154 0, at identical page counts 124 of 154 is 81 % of the corpus rendering differently while the barometer does not flicker. The witness for those changes is the oracle — \hbox{AV} at 10pt in Libertinus measured 13.47pt against XeTeX’s 12.35pt and now measures 12.35pt; the whole \tiny…\Huge ladder read out of the PDF’s own Tf matches tectonic entry for entry. The tool that sees this already existed and says so itself; what was missing is that the routine sweep does not run it (engine#716).
Running heads are the clearest case of a change this barometer cannot report. A page’s head is produced by \mark, and \mark is a node: TeX carries the material to the output routine and fire_up derives the three quantities a head is written from (tex.web:19718-19729, :19782-19789) — \topmark is the previous page’s \botmark, \firstmark is this page’s first mark or else \topmark, and \botmark is this page’s last mark and is not cleared on a page that carries none, which is what makes a head persist across a chapter. On top of that latex.ltx keeps the left/right pair in one token list, \@themark (ltpage.dtx:355), with \leftmark and \rightmark reading \botmark and \firstmark through \@firstoftwo/\@secondoftwo (:167-174, :341-342) — and \@markright deliberately keeps the left half, which is why \markright in a \section does not erase the chapter.
The effect: 27 of the 128 corpus papers that have a reference PDF now get the head they had been missing, and the whole change moves Σ|deviation| by zero, because a head replaces blank space in a running header that was already reserved. Only a per-page hash sees it.
It took four fixes, three of them correct and insufficient. A one-line substrate stub, \def\mark#1{}, silently discarded its argument and sat one layer below all three — so each correct fix above it changed nothing observable and each looked wrong. What found it was not a better fix but a different question: a test that asks whether the node arrives, rather than whether the layer that emits it is right (engine#426, engine#729). Any stub that accepts input and drops it will outlive every repair made above it. a geometry check, which is the only one of the three that can see text drawn outside the sheet. A block that should fill a title page used to be set as one horizontal list that was never line-broken, so everything past the right margin was placed off the paper — up to x=6619pt on a 612pt page, author names, affiliations and e-mails among it. The page count cannot see that (the clearest witness is 15 pages against 15), the ink count cannot (every glyph is emitted) and the text layer carries the words. Measured as lines ending beyond any page width this corpus uses: 49 papers at v0.260.0, 23 at v0.261.0, 22 at v0.262.0, against a floor of 2 on the reference PDFs themselves. The widest line went from 6619pt at v0.260.0 to 3357pt at v0.261.0 and 1788pt at v0.262.0.
a render check: a sha256 over the bytes of every page’s SVG, so it covers every coordinate on the page. Every sweep had recorded one since the beginning and nothing had ever compared two, so the page-count comparisons were the only ones being read — and they are blind by construction to anything that moves material within a page. That blindness reports such a change as “no document moved”, which reads as the change does nothing when the truth is the instrument cannot see it. Seven changes measured since: 2, 25, 72, 40, 72, 18 and 73 of the 154 corpus documents render differently; across the first six exactly one document moved by a page (engine#675). That one is worth the sentence it takes: 2209.13121 went 36 pages to 37 against a reference of 42, so Σ|deviation| fell 277 → 276 while the signed bias rose +49 → +50 — the bias rose because the paper was short, not because anything got worse. The seventh is the exception that shows what the channel is for: 73 render differently and 14 moved by a page, which is the first change here whose page-count effect was worth reading on its own — and even there 59 of the 73 were invisible to it. It answers did the output change, not is it better: the reference’s PDFs are not our SVGs, so there is no third hash to be right about.

data.pipeline-stages#Pipeline stages:
Each stage is gated by an objective oracle.
Stage Status What it covers Mouth + gullet ✅ done Category-code tokenizer, eqtb, macros (delimited parameters, full expansion), conditionals, registers, grouping. Stomach ✅ done Box/glue/penalty model in scaled points, Knuth–Plass line breaking, a cost-based page builder that keeps TeX’s two page measurements apart — page_total, which the break is decided on, and page_depth, which is not charged against the goal and is capped at \maxdepth — and \halign tables. Math ✅ done $…$ and display environments delegated to math (vector output). Fonts ✅ done OpenType via go-opentype; a built-in default font, kerning and ligatures — runs with no assets. The size ladder is the class’s own table to the point: all ten of \tiny…\Huge match tectonic, including \Large 14.4, \LARGE 17.28 and \huge 20.74. Output ✅ done PDF (embedded subset fonts, selectable text) and self-contained SVG pages with a click-to-line source map. Real classes ✅ done \documentclass{article|report|book} loads and runs the genuine embedded LaTeX class, native and js/wasm.
data.roadmap#Roadmap:
The engine loads and runs the standard base classes; it is functional-parity-oriented and held to real-LaTeX fidelity, not a claim of full TeXLive parity.
Heavy packages (tikz, …) run as real files rather than native stubs; TikZ/pgf drawing is gated behind GOTEX_PGF and in bring-up.
Front matter that still reaches past the page edge: 22 of the 154 corpus papers, down from 49, with five causes closed and the remainder a different population each (engine#629). The fifth cause is \unvbox inside a paragraph: a vbox holds finished lines, and handing them to the line breaker glues them end to end and re-breaks the lot as one paragraph (acmart writes \noindent\unvbox\mktitle@bx).
How far from the kernel, measured. latex.ltx — the assembled LaTeX kernel tectonic itself executes — defines 1952 control sequences. This engine and go-tex/math carry 755 of them; 1197 are absent, of which 642 are written by at least one paper in the 21 956-paper corpus. That is the shape of “not full TeXLive parity”, in numbers rather than in a disclaimer (engine#677). The list is a reading order, not a defect list. An earlier reading of the same inventory put it at 1256 absent and 695 used: the difference is three asymmetries in the reader, each of which made the engine look poorer than it is, and each found by taking three names off the head and checking them by hand.
Ranking the absences by corpus demand turned out to rank noise. The first fourteen entries are names this engine already writes down somewhere — a special case in Go (\multicolumn, 51 of the 154 measured papers, is supported without being defined), a test file of its own (\baselinestretch, 41), or a comment saying why the name is deliberately absent (\@evenfoot and \@evenhead, 42 and 41: this engine has no two-sided page model). \do (46) is a loop hook every caller \lets to its own action. The measurement tool now marks such a name cited — absent as a definition, but already thought about — and 221 of the 642 used absences are cited. Nothing is filtered: the citation is a column beside the demand, because dropping a cited name would be a false presence, and a false presence deletes work for good where a false absence costs one reading.
The list has no safe head, and that is the useful thing it says. The first absence this engine writes down nowhere at all is \@citea/\@citeb, 18 of the 154 — and defining them would accomplish nothing: they are the loop variables of \@citex, which this engine never executes, \cite being written in Go. A name internal to a macro replaced wholesale is invisible to both tests, and only reading the caller finds it. The defect in that neighbourhood is a real one of a familiar shape — a class’s \@biblabel and \@cite were executed into the eqtb and then ignored, exactly as \footnoterule used to be, now closed — but it is not the one the ranking named. Every entry on this list needs its caller read before it is believed.
Walked to the end, both tables, the inventory yielded two changes the corpus can see — the footnote’s layout and the citation’s brackets — and nothing else. The rest is error machinery, internals of macros this engine replaces in Go, and one declared \halign limitation (\omit/\span) whose own code comment already carries the measurement saying it changes nothing here: all 282 of the corpus’s \halign uses sit in files the engine substitutes rather than executes, and compiling a paper that ships one never reaches the word. Those are conformance work — they are TeX primitives, and \halign{…\omit…} is an abort today — but no fidelity number justifies them. So the next work comes from the measured channels above, not from the inventory; it stays open as a record of five ways an inventory can mislead, not as a queue.
A footnote is laid out by its class. The mark is whatever \thefootnote expands to, so \renewcommand\thefootnote{\fnsymbol{footnote}} works and a title block’s \thanks comes out ∗; and the note itself is now built by calling the class’s \@makefntext instead of placing the mark in Go, so the 1.8em box that right-aligns it (article.cls:609-612) is there. Before, every note’s text began one box-width to the left of the reference’s: no box of 14.400pt existed anywhere on the page, and one does now. What remains is the mark’s size: \@textsuperscript is the identity here, so it is set on the baseline at text size where the reference raises it, and \@fnsymbol gives an ASCII * where the reference sets * in math mode and draws U+2217.
A citation’s brackets belong to the class too. \@biblabel and \@cite are macros in the reference (latex.ltx:13324, :13322), and article.cls:568 builds the bibliography list’s label by calling \@biblabel. They were brackets built in Go, so a class’s redefinition reached the eqtb — this engine runs real .cls files — and was dropped at the point of use: a document writing \def\@biblabel#1{<<#1>>} rendered byte-identically to one that did not. 22 of the 154 carry a class that redefines one of the two, and since only 50 of the 154 ship a class at all, that is 44 % of the papers that bring their own; 18 of 154 render differently. \@citex — the iteration natbib replaces by \letting it — is not executed: exactly one paper in 154 ships natbib.sty, and no number calls for running the real package in place of the Go emulation (engine#681).
⛔ That last clause was wrong, and the number that refutes it is a different count. “One paper ships natbib.sty” is about papers that carry the file. 20 of the 154 \usepackage{natbib}, and none of those twenty ships it — so all twenty fall back to the Go emulation, where \citet loses the author name outright: “obtained by [27]” where LaTeX writes “obtained by Nordbotten et al. [27]”. Rendering one of them with the real package on the search path changes 285 diff lines. A measured claim can be true and still answer a question nobody asked; this one counted shipping when the thing that matters is loading.
The engine can now run the real package: \@auxout was \def\@auxout{-1}, a number no \openout ever opens, so everything natbib wrote to the .aux went nowhere. With it a real stream carried across passes (engine#712), \citep/\citet in authoryear mode produce word for word what tectonic produces, with no undefined commands skipped. What is left is reaching the file (engine#703): CTAN ships natbib as docstrip source with no natbib.sty in the archive and no .tds.zip at all.
6.1pt of leftover on a page that stretches. With vertical infinite glue now contributing and every page packed exactly to \vsize, \vspace{\fill} puts its word at y=658.6 against tectonic’s 664.7 — the remaining third of (engine#663), which described three defects under one title.
A \marginpar’s note is read but not placed in the margin. Its arguments no longer reach the page as text and the body matches the reference exactly; putting the note itself out in the margin goes through LaTeX’s float machinery and is still to come.
A broader real-document conformance corpus (PDF-diff against pdftex/xetex) and the TRIP test.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
Runs the standard base classes for real. article, report and book load and execute the genuine embedded LaTeX .cls files, typesetting a numbered title, a 	ableofcontents shaped by the class’s own \l@… macros (the indent and number-box widths are read out of its \@dottedtocline calls, so article’s leaderless bold \l@section and book’s dotted one at the same level come out differently), numbered sections/subsections, \chapter (report/book, with its entry in the contents list and its opening page’s folio at the foot), numbered figure/table captions, itemize/enumerate, and math. A full pipeline. A category-code mouth and gullet, a scaled-point stomach with Knuth–Plass line breaking and a cost-based page builder, \halign tables, math via math (vector output), OpenType fonts (a built-in default font, kerning, ligatures), and PDF + SVG output — the SVG carries a source map for click-to-line. Floats and two columns are the default. Real float placement (top, bottom and float-page, with the seven parameters read from the class rather than from article’s) and the two-column layouts that classes set themselves (revtex reprint, acmart sigconf/sigplan, IEEEtran) are on without a flag; GOTEX_FLOATS=0 and GOTEX_TWOCOLUMN=0 opt back out. This page described both as still behind their environment variables, which they have not been for some time. Spacing and breaking commands behave as LaTeX’s own. \hspace and \vspace take a glue, not a rigid length, so \hspace{ ill}, \vspace{\stretch{2}} and \hspace{1cm plus 2mm} keep their stretch;  ill, \stretch, \enskip and \samepage are defined, with  ill and \stretch at the reference’s second order of infinity. \pagebreak, 
opagebreak, \linebreak and 
olinebreak contribute the penalties LaTeX gives them, the optional degree [0…4] included. \marginpar reads both of its arguments instead of letting them reach the page as text. (v0.263.1) \ carries its star and its optional length, and \vadjust works. \[20pt] used to typeset the five characters [20pt] and \* a *; both are now scanned, and the length produces the reference’s 31.88pt baseline step where a bare \ gives 11.96. \vadjust{…} puts vertical material written inside a paragraph into the enclosing vertical list after the line it was written on — measured against tectonic as a 41.84pt step against a normal 11.96 — and it is an error in vertical mode, as TeX requires. Two commands came with it: \pagebreak and 
opagebreak now work when written on a line and not only between paragraphs (the reference makes two pages on a short first paragraph, and so do we, where we made one), and \* refuses a page break after its line. In the browser. A self-contained js/wasm build renders real LaTeX classes client-side — no TeXLive, no server.

data.tex#tex:
A lightweight, pure-Go (CGO_ENABLED=0) processor for a practical subset of LaTeX documents. It tokenizes with TeX category codes, expands user macros (\newcommand/\renewcommand with mandatory and optional arguments, \def, \let), parses document structure, and emits semantic HTML with math typeset by math. No engine binary, no cgo, no server; it compiles to GOOS=js/wasm.
For full TeX — real line breaking, page building, the LaTeX classes, and PDF/SVG output — see engine; tex is a lightweight document-to-HTML path.
